title: Methodus nova et facilis calculum variationum tractandi

deep.reconstruction:
The page finishes §3 and gives §§4–5 of E420 (Novi Commentarii 16, 1771/72).

§3 (end): In his earlier treatment, the old Lagrange–Euler δ-calculus, Euler gave y, besides its ordinary differential dy, a second increment δy. This increment is entirely arbitrary and not determined by x. He called it the 'variation' and gave rules for propagating it through expressions of three kinds:
(i) functions of x and y;
(ii) functions also containing p = dy/dx, q = dp/dx, and so on;
(iii) expressions containing integrals ∫V dx.

§4: The calculus of variations therefore seemed a wholly singular kind of calculus. On closer study Euler sees that, after a slight change, the whole of it reduces to the 'second part' of the integral calculus. He set out that part in volume 3 of the Institutiones calculi integralis (1770): integration of functions of two variables, i.e. partial differential equations. He adds that this branch had so far scarcely got beyond its first elements.

§5: Instead of an abstract increment δy, take y as a function of two independent variables x and t. Then:
- dx(∂y/∂x) is the true differential of y;
- dt(∂y/∂t) plays the role of the old δy.

Geometrically, y is the ordinate of a curve over abscissa x. The variational calculus needs a relation that captures all neighbouring curves. If X is the given function, these are contained in y = X + tV, where V is an arbitrary function of x.

Next page: with t infinitely small, this family contains all nearby curves. More generally one may take any y(x,t) with y(x,0) = X. The variation of Z(x,y) is then N dt(∂y/∂t), where N = ∂Z/∂y. In modern terms, δF = (d/dt) F[y(·,t)] at t = 0, i.e. the Gateaux derivative along a one-parameter family of admissible functions (the 'ε-family' method of modern textbooks).
errors: No mathematical errors on this page.

Taking t 'infinitely small' to get all neighbouring curves is the usual infinitesimal idiom. Strictly, the family X + tV for a fixed V is one direction only; it is the arbitrariness of V that covers every neighbouring curve, which Euler does say.
The neighbouring page's printed section numbering repeats '7' (the first should be 6). This is a printing or transcription slip, not a mathematical one.

ideas.what: Replace the formal symbol δ by a partial derivative with respect to an auxiliary parameter t: δy = dt (∂y/∂t), where y = y(x,t).
ideas.modern_name: First variation as a derivative along a one-parameter family (Gateaux derivative; embedding/variation of a curve)
ideas.usually_credited_to: Euler, E420 (1771/72) and the appendix to Institutiones calculi integralis III (E385, 1770); later standard via Lagrange, Jacobi and Weierstrass-era textbooks
ideas.where_published: E420 itself; E385 appendix to Inst. calc. int. vol. III; discussed by Goldstine (History of the Calculus of Variations), Fraser (articles on Euler's reformulation), and the Opera omnia I.25 introduction (Carathéodory)

ideas.what: Family of comparison curves y = X + tV with V arbitrary, generalised to any y(x,t) with y(x,0) = X.
ideas.modern_name: Admissible variations / ε-family of comparison functions
ideas.usually_credited_to: Euler (this paper); standard in later textbooks

ideas.what: Claim that the calculus of variations reduces to the theory of functions of two variables (partial differential calculus, Inst. calc. int. III).
ideas.modern_name: Reduction of variational calculus to partial differentiation

deep.surprise_reason: This is Euler's well-known reinterpretation of δ as ∂/∂t along a one-parameter family. It is thoroughly documented in the histories of the calculus of variations (Goldstine, Fraser, Carathéodory's Opera omnia introduction). Nothing on the page appears absent from the literature.
